quotes.text: The album was self-produced by the band on purpose. They only wanted an engineer "who can put their technical knowledge into what we want, the way we want it. He's got to take us as we are". They recorded it live in the studio as "basic" as possible with "no overdubs to speak of"; Ferguson explained, "The mixing is where the difference is".
The album's lyrics were written by Coleman and Ferguson expressing their opinions on issues such as politics, death, hypocrisy, human nature, pollution and exile.
It's a weird mash of genres: proto-industrial, post-punk, metal... But the mix works.
Ahead of their time sound-wise, hard to believe this was 1980. A good mixture of punk and more melodic.

The repetitive character of the guitar riffs, the keystrokes and the rousing drumwork have an hypnotic effect on the music, and musically and lyrically it provides a somewhat nihilistic and grey view of the world.
It is the link between the punk and the post-punk.
Killing Joke succeeds in creating a the atmosphere and sound that is characteristic of the British urban environments in the early 1980s.
It felt about 10 years ahead of its time as its influence on industrial metal and alternative rock are immediately clear.
The album was self-produced by the band on purpose. They only wanted an engineer "who can put their technical knowledge into what we want, the way we want it. He's got to take us as we are".
They recorded it live in the studio as "basic" as possible with "no overdubs to speak of"; Ferguson explained, "The mixing is where the difference is".
Since 1980, there have been a hundred bands who sound like this, but before Steve Albini and Al Jourgensen made it hip, the cold metallic throb of Killing Joke was exciting and fresh.
In the band's biography it was called an "outstanding debut album which captured not only their defining sound, but also the chilling apocalyptic anguish about the world to come."
The music critic Chuck Eddy has praised the album for its "surprisingly potent gridlock-plot avant-drone somberness, layers of fuzz over kamikaze electrobongos".
There is nothing phony, gimmicky or pretentious about this record or this band. Simplicity: powerful riffs and gang choruses over undeniable grooves. Nobody, nobody, did this before. Pure innovation.
it would be fair to say Killing Joke were one of the most pivotal and influential bands of the whole post-punk era.

many would argue that even during their lifetime, Killing Joke themselves struggled to repeat the halcyon days of their first three albums, despite many years and experimental diversions in pursuit of trying.

rather than reminisce about the past in the hope of some second coming of 'Psyche' or whatever, they've defied all expectations and created arguably their most definitive, and overtly complex body of work in decades.
it's undoubtedly the unnerving tension and perpetual antagonism that's partly responsible for a record many thought this time last year was little more than a romantic pipe dream.

All the key elements of Killing Joke mk.I remain intact; Jaz Coleman's infectious growl, Geordie Walker's signature guitar reverberations, Youth's dub-tinged basslines and the pounding brutality of Paul Ferguson behind the drumkit.
From the opening riff of the introductory six-minute long title track, Absolute Dissent is a relentless assault that hints at Killing Joke's past but suggests an altogether heavier approach.
such is their tenacity in striving for perfection Absolute Dissent rarely falls short of the mark.
Absolute Dissent is a remarkable achievement for a band whose creative zenith appeared to have been locked in the annals many moons ago.
But then this band have never been about taking the conventional approach.
What could have been a fitting epitaph for the band has instead refuelled their creative fires.

For a band shortly entering its thirty-fifth year they could be forgiven for simply reverting to formula. However, the newly revitalised Killing Joke have taken the bull by the horns as it were and delivered a record that is up there with their finest.

MMXII, or '2012', is a devastating slab of industrial rock loosely based around the Mayan concept whereby the twenty-first of December 2012 will signify the end of time. Intelligently researched and politically charged throughout, MMXII delivers a ten-part suckerpunch in brutal fashion.
As with MMXII's predecessor, the band have taken on production duties themselves, again enlisting Clive Goddard on the mixing and engineering side of things.
Now whittled down from 26 to ten pieces, MMXII makes its intentions clear from the outset, 'Pole Shift' introducing the record via a cascading symphony of vibrating bass and thunderous synths.
Musically taut throughout its nine minutes, Geordie's signature guitar scaling omnipresent, it's a blistering opener that sets the pace for what follows.

With the metallic sound more prevalent here than on Absolute Dissent, there's little wonder people like Dave Grohl and Trent Reznor were queuing up to provide plaudits on their forthcoming documentary and celluloid debut The Death and Resurrection Show.
Lead single 'In Cythera' is perhaps the most direct throwback to their past, sounding not a million miles away from 1986's long forgotten 'Adorations'.

The penultimate 'Trance' also offers a nod to times gone by, its rumbling bassline mirroring that of early release 'Pssyche', while Geordie concocts his most abrasive guitar scripture this side of their comeback.
Perhaps surprisingly choosing to go out with a reflective sigh than an almighty thud, 'On All Hallow's Eve' represents three minutes of Killing Joke at their most emotionally charged.

The sound of a band still in their creative prime, MMXII is everything Killing Joke have proclaimed themselves to be these past three-and-a-half decades, and 15 albums on is just as incisive and coarse as their debut.
